question.text:
$x$ $1$ $2$ $3$ $4$
$f(x)$ $0.5$ $0.2$ $0.1$ $0.2$

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_{50}$ be a random sample of size $n = 50$ from a population with the probability mass function given above. Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is greater than $2.2.$

Note: $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.
question.explanation:
Suppose that $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma.$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ can be approximated as

\[ \overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right). \]

In our case:

  • the sample size is \begin{align*} n &= 50, \end{align*}

  • the population mean is \begin{align*} \mu &= \textrm{E}[X] \\[5pt] &= \sum_{i=1}^n x_i f(x_i) \\[5pt] &= 1 \cdot 0.5 + 2 \cdot 0.2 + 3\cdot 0.1 + 4 \cdot 0.2 \\[5pt] &= 0.5 + 0.4 + 0.3 + 0.8 \\[5pt] &= 2, \end{align*}

  • the population variance is \begin{align*} \sigma^2 &= \textrm{Var}[X] \\[5pt] &=\textrm{E}[X^2]−\textrm{E}[X]^2 \\[5pt] &= \big( 1^2\cdot 0.5+2^2\cdot0.2+3^2\cdot 0.1+4^2\cdot 0.2 \big) − 2^2 \\[5pt] &= \big( 0.5 + 0.8 + 0.9 + 3.2 \big) - 4 \\[5pt] &=1.4. \end{align*}

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

\begin{align*} \overline{X} &\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right) \\[5pt] &\sim N\!\left(2, \dfrac{1.4}{50}\right) \\[5pt] &\sim N(2, 0.028). \end{align*}

We want to find $P(\overline{X} \gt 2.2).$ So, we convert $\overline{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\begin{align} P(\overline{X} > 2.2) &\approx P\left (Z > \dfrac{2.2-2}{\sqrt{0.028}}\right) \\[5pt] &=P(Z > 1.20) \\[5pt] &=1 - \Phi(1.20). \end{align}

Therefore, we conclude that

\[ P(\overline{X} > 2.2) = 1 - \Phi(1.20). \]

question.text:
Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_{50}$ be a random sample of size $n=50$ from a population with probability density function \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{5}{x^6}, & x \geq 1, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Given that the population variance $\sigma^2 =0.1,$ calculate $P( \overline{X} < 1.2).$

Hint: A table of values of $\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

$z$$\, 0.01 \,$$\, 0.02 \,$$\, 0.03 \,$
$\, -1.2 \,$ $\, 0.1131 \,$ $\, 0.1112 \,$ $\, 0.1093 \,$
$\, -1.1 \,$ $\, 0.1335 \,$ $\, 0.1314 \,$ $\, 0.1292 \,$
$\, -1.0 \,$ $\, 0.1562 \,$ $\, 0.1539 \,$ $\, 0.1515 \,$
question.explanation:
Suppose that $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma.$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ can be approximated as

\[ \overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right). \]

In our case:

  • the sample size is \begin{align*} n &= 50, \end{align*}

  • the population mean is \begin{align*} \mu &= \textrm{E}[X] \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x \, f(x) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{\infty} x\cdot \dfrac{5}{x^6} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{\infty} \dfrac{5}{x^5} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \lim_{b\to\infty}\int_{1}^{b} \dfrac{5}{x^5} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \lim_{b\to\infty}\left[-\dfrac{5}{4x^4}\right]_{1}^{b} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{4}\\[5pt] &=1.25, \end{align*}

  • the population variance is $\sigma^2 = 0.1.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

\begin{align*} \overline{X} &\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right) \\[5pt] &\sim N\!\left(1.25, \dfrac{0.1}{50}\right) \\[5pt] &\sim N(1.25, 0.002). \end{align*}

We want to find $P(\overline{X} < 1.2).$ So, we convert $\overline{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\begin{align} P\left( \overline{X}< 1.2\right) &= P\left ( Z < \dfrac{1.2-1.25}{\sqrt{0.002}} \right) \\[5pt] &\approx P\left ( Z < -1.12\right)\\[5pt] &=\Phi(-1.12) \end{align}

From the table, we have that \[ \Phi(-1.12) = 0.1314. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align} P\left( \overline{X} < 1.2\right) &=\Phi(-1.12)\\[5pt] &=0.1314. \end{align}

example.title: Using the CLT With a Population Whose Probability Distribution Is Continuous

question.text:
Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_{55}$ be a random sample of size $n=55$ from a population with probability density function \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{4}x^3, & 0 \leq x \leq 2, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Given that the population variance $\sigma^2 = 0.11,$ calculate $P(1.6 < \overline{X} < 1.7).$

Hint: A table of values of $\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

$z$$\, 0.02 \,$$\, 0.03 \,$$\, 0.04 \,$
$\, 2.0 \,$ $\, 0.9783 \,$ $\, 0.9788 \,$ $\, 0.9793 \,$
$\, 2.1 \,$ $\, 0.9830 \,$ $\, 0.9834 \,$ $\, 0.9838 \,$
$\, 2.2 \,$ $\, 0.9868 \,$ $\, 0.9871 \,$ $\, 0.9875 \,$
question.explanation:
Suppose that $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma.$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ can be approximated as

\[ \overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right). \]

In our case:

  • the sample size is \begin{align*} n &=55, \end{align*}

  • the population mean is \begin{align*} \mu &= \textrm{E}[X] \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x \, f(x) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^2 x\cdot \dfrac{1}{4} x^3 \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^2 \dfrac{1}{4}x^4 \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[\dfrac{x^5}{20}\right]_{0}^{2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{32}{20}\\[5pt] &= 1.6, \end{align*}

  • the population variance is $\sigma^2 = 0.11.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

\begin{align*} \overline{X} &\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right) \\[5pt] &\sim N\!\left(1.6, \dfrac{0.11}{55}\right) \\[5pt] &\sim N(1.6, 0.002). \end{align*}

We want to find $P(1.6 < \overline{X} < 1.7).$ So, we convert $\overline{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\begin{align} P\left(1.6 < \overline{X} < 1.7\right) &= P\left (\dfrac{1.6-1.6}{\sqrt{0.002}} < Z < \dfrac{1.7-1.6}{\sqrt{0.002}} \right) \\[5pt] &\approx P\left (0 < Z < 2.24\right)\\[5pt] &=P\left (Z < 2.24\right)-P\left (Z < 0\right)\\[5pt] &=\Phi(2.24)-\Phi(0) \end{align}

From the table, we have \[ \Phi(2.24) = 0.9875, \]

and by the symmetry of the normal distribution, $\Phi(0) = 0.5.$ Therefore,

\begin{align} P(1.6 < \overline{X} < 1.7) &=\Phi(2.24)-\Phi(0)\\[5pt] &=0.9875 - 0.5\\[5pt] &=0.4875. \end{align}

example.title: Using the CLT With a Population Whose Probability Distribution Is Continuous

question.text:
Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_{30}$ be a random sample of size $n=30$ from a population with probability density function \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} 4x^3, & 0 \leq x \leq 1, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Given that the population variance $\sigma^2 = 0.03,$ calculate $P( \overline{X} > 0.7).$

Hint: A table of values of $\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

$z$$\, 0.04 \,$$\, 0.05 \,$$\, 0.06 \,$
$\, -3.2 \,$ $\, 0.0006 \,$ $\, 0.0006 \,$ $\, 0.0006 \,$
$\, -3.1 \,$ $\, 0.0008 \,$ $\, 0.0008 \,$ $\, 0.0008 \,$
$\, -3.0 \,$ $\, 0.0012 \,$ $\, 0.0011 \,$ $\, 0.0011 \,$
question.explanation:
Suppose that $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma.$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ can be approximated as

\[ \overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right). \]

In our case:

  • the sample size is \begin{align*} n &= 30, \end{align*}

  • the population mean is \begin{align*} \mu &= \textrm{E}[X] \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x \, f(x) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^1 x\cdot 4x^3 \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^1 4x^4 \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[\dfrac{4x^5}{5}\right]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{4}{5}\\[5pt] &= 0.8, \end{align*}

  • the population variance is $\sigma^2 = 0.03.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

\begin{align*} \overline{X} &\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right) \\[5pt] &\sim N\!\left(0.8, \dfrac{0.03}{30}\right) \\[5pt] &\sim N(0.8, 0.001). \end{align*}

We want to find $P( \overline{X} > 0.7).$ So, we convert $\overline{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\begin{align} P\left(\overline{X} > 0.7\right) &= P\left ( Z > \dfrac{0.7-0.8}{\sqrt{0.001}} \right) \\[5pt] &\approx P\left ( Z > -3.16\right) \end{align}

Using the complement of the normal distribution, we have \begin{align} P\left ( Z > -3.16 \right) & = 1 - P(Z \lt -3.16) \\[5pt] & = 1 - \Phi(-3.16). \end{align}

From the table, we have that

\[ \Phi(-3.16) = 0.0008. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align} P( \overline{X} > 0.7 ) &=1-\Phi(-3.16)\\[5pt] &=1- 0.0008\\[5pt] &=0.9992. \end{align}

question.text:
$x$ $1$ $4$ $6$ $8$
$f(x)$ $0.4$ $0.25$ $0.1$ $0.25$

Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{128}$ be a random sample of size $n = 128$ from a population with the probability mass function given above. Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is between $3.6$ and $4.2.$

Hint: Two tables of values of $\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ are given below, where $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

$z$ $\, 0.00 \,$ $\, 0.01 \,$ $\, 0.02 \,$
$\, 0.7\,$ $\,0.7580 \,$ $\,0.7611 \,$ $\,0.7642 \,$
$\, 0.8 \,$ $\,0.7881 \,$ $\,0.7910 \,$ $\,0.7939 \,$
$\, 0.9 \,$ $\, 0.8159 \,$ $\, 0.8186 \,$ $\, 0.8212 \,$

$z$ $\, 0.00 \,$ $\, 0.01 \,$ $\, 0.02 \,$
$\, -1.7\,$ $\,0.0446 \,$ $\,0.0436 \,$ $\,0.0427 \,$
$\, -1.6 \,$ $\,0.0548 \,$ $\,0.0537 \,$ $\,0.0526 \,$
$\, -1.5 \,$ $\, 0.0668 \,$ $\, 0.0655 \,$ $\, 0.0643 \,$
question.explanation:
Suppose that $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu$ and population standard deviation $\sigma.$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ can be approximated as

\[ \overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right). \]

In our case:

  • the sample size is \[ n = 128, \]

  • the population mean is \begin{align*} \mu &= \textrm{E}[X] \\[5pt] &= \sum_{i=1}^n x_i f(x_i) \\[5pt] &= 1 \cdot 0.4 + 4 \cdot 0.25+ 6 \cdot 0.1 + 8 \cdot 0.25 \\[5pt] &= 0.4 + 1 + 0.6 + 2 \\[5pt] &= 4, \end{align*}

  • the population variance is \begin{align*} \sigma^2 &= \textrm{Var}[X] \\[5pt] &= \textrm{E}[X^2]−\textrm{E}[X]^2 \\[5pt] &= \big( 1^2 \cdot 0.4 + 4^2 \cdot 0.25+ 6^2 \cdot 0.1 + 8^2 \cdot 0.25\big) − 4^2 \\[5pt] &= \big( 0.4 + 4 + 3.6 + 16\big) - 16 \\[5pt] &= 8. \end{align*}

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

\begin{align*} \overline{X} &\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right) \\[5pt] &\sim N\!\left(4, \dfrac{8}{128}\right) \\[5pt] &\sim N(4, 0.0625). \end{align*}

We want to find $P(3.6 \lt \overline{X} \lt 4.2).$ So, we convert $\overline{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\begin{align} P(3.6 \lt \overline{X} \lt 4.2) &\approx - P\left (\dfrac{3.6-4}{\sqrt{0.0625}}\lt Z \lt \dfrac{4.2-4}{\sqrt{0.0625}}\right) \\[5pt] &\approx - P\left (-1.6\lt Z \lt 0.8\right) \\[5pt] &= P(Z \lt 0.8) - P(Z \lt -1.6) \\[5pt] &= \Phi(0.8) - \Phi(-1.6) . \end{align}

From the tables, we have \begin{align} \Phi(0.8) = 0.7881,\\[5pt] \Phi(-1.6) =0.0548. \end{align}

Therefore, \begin{align} P(3.6 \lt \overline{X} \lt 4.2) &= \Phi(0.8) - \Phi(-1.6) \\[5pt] &= 0.7881 - 0.0548 \\[5pt] &= 0.7333. \end{align}
